claim: Full-length mRNAs transfer between adjacent mammalian cells via direct cell-to-cell connections called tunneling nanotubes (TNTs).
source: Full-length mRNAs transfer between adjacent mammalian cells via direct cell-to-cell connections called tunneling nanotubes (TNTs).
evidence: This is a statement of established finding from prior work by the authors, supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: mRNA transfer is non-selective and prevalent across the human transcriptome.
source: We found that mRNA transfer is non-selective, prevalent across the human transcriptome, and that the amount of transfer to mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs) strongly correlates with the endogenous level of gene expression in donor human breast cancer cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-sequencing data showing transfer of nearly all mRNAs (Figure 2A, 2C) and lack of specific motifs (Figure 5-figure supplements 1 and 2).

claim: The amount of mRNA transfer to mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs) strongly correlates with the endogenous level of gene expression in donor human breast cancer cells.
source: We found that mRNA transfer is non-selective, prevalent across the human transcriptome, and that the amount of transfer to mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs) strongly correlates with the endogenous level of gene expression in donor human breast cancer cells.
evidence: This is supported by linear regression analysis showing Pearson and Spearman coefficients >0.9 (Figure 2E-G).

claim: Typically, <1% of endogenous mRNAs undergo transfer.
source: Typically,<1% of endogenous mRNAs undergo transfer.
evidence: This is supported by the median percentage of transfer being 0.34% (Figure 3A).

claim: RNA transfer appears contact-dependent via TNTs.
source: RNA transfer appears contact-dependent via TNTs, as exemplified for several mRNAs.
evidence: This is supported by quadrapod and conditioned media experiments (Figure 6-figure supplement 1) and FISH imaging showing mRNAs in TNTs (Figure 6).

claim: Significant differential changes in the native MEF transcriptome were observed in response to co-culture, including the upregulation of multiple cancer and cancer-associated fibroblast-related genes and pathways.
source: Notably, significant differential changes in the native MEF transcriptome were observed in response to co-culture, including the upregulation of multiple cancer and cancer-associated fibroblast-related genes and pathways.
evidence: This is supported by differential gene expression analysis showing >4000 differentially expressed genes (Figure 7C) and overlap with CAF markers (Figure 8).

claim: Initial evidence of intercellular transfer of RNA was found in the early 1970s (Kolodny, 1971; Kolodny, 1972).
source: Although initial evidence of the intercellular transfer of RNA was found in the early 1970s (Kolodny, 1971; Kolodny, 1972), the mechanism of transfer gained attention much later.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to historical literature.

claim: The prevalent mechanism by which RNAs are thought to be transferred is through extracellular vesicles (EVs), which include apoptotic bodies, microvesicles and exosomes.
source: The prevalent mechanism by which RNAs are thought to be transferred is through extracellular vesicles (EVs), which include apoptotic bodies, microvesicles and exosomes.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific consensus in the field.

claim: Exosomes are vesicles of endocytic origin with sizes ranging from 40 to 100 nm and can transfer information in the form of proteins, lipids, DNA and RNA (O'Brien et al., 2020).
source: Best studied are exosomes, which are vesicles of endocytic origin with sizes ranging from 40 to 100 nm and can transfer information in the form of proteins, lipids, DNA and RNA (O'Brien et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: Exosomes are released by numerous cell types (e.g. immune cells, neuronal and cancer cells Mittelbrunn et al., 2011; Villarroya-Beltri et al., 2013).
source: Released by numerous cell types (e.g. immune cells, neuronal and cancer cells Mittelbrunn et al., 2011; Villarroya-Beltri et al., 2013), they are secreted into extracellular media and body fluids (e.g. saliva, blood plasma, breast milk, and urine) (Zhang et al., 2019b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Exosomes are secreted into extracellular media and body fluids (e.g. saliva, blood plasma, breast milk, and urine) (Zhang et al., 2019b).
source: Released by numerous cell types (e.g. immune cells, neuronal and cancer cells Mittelbrunn et al., 2011; Villarroya-Beltri et al., 2013), they are secreted into extracellular media and body fluids (e.g. saliva, blood plasma, breast milk, and urine) (Zhang et al., 2019b).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation.

claim: Multiple species of RNAs are present in exosomes (e.g. snoRNA, siRNA, Y-RNA, lncRNA, and vault RNA).
source: Profiling of their RNA content using DNA microarrays or RNA sequencing has revealed that while multiple species of RNAs are present in exosomes (e.g. snoRNA, siRNA, Y-RNA, lncRNA, and vault RNA), work has mainly focused on microRNAs (miRs; Li et al., 2014; Valadi et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies profiling exosomal RNA content.

claim: GFP mRNA in exosomes was taken up by a colon cancer cell line and translated (Jiang et al., 2015).
source: One report found that GFP mRNA in exosomes was taken up by a colon cancer cell line and translated (Jiang et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a specific study.

claim: Only small sized RNAs (e.g. miRs) and fragments of mRNA are likely to be enriched in the exosomes (Batagov and Kurochkin, 2013; Pérez-Boza et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2018).
source: However, exosomes may not be the sole agent by which RNAs transfer from one cell to another. In fact, multiple studies show that only small sized RNAs (e.g. miRs) and fragments of mRNA are likely to be enriched in the exosomes (Batagov and Kurochkin, 2013; Pérez-Boza et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Exosomes may not be the preferred mode of full-length mRNA transport between cells.
source: Thus, exosomes may not be the preferred mode of full-length mRNA transport between cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited evidence that exosomes primarily contain small RNAs and mRNA fragments.

claim: ARC and PEG10 mRNAs encode proteins that can form retroviral-like capsids and package their own mRNAs for transfer to neighboring cells (Ashley et al., 2018; Pastuzyn et al., 2018; Segel et al., 2021).
source: Interestingly, ARC and PEG10 mRNAs encode proteins that can form retroviral-like capsids and package their own mRNAs for transfer to neighboring cells (Ashley et al., 2018; Pastuzyn et al., 2018; Segel et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Retroviral-like capsid-mediated transfer is probably limited to a small set of mRNAs encoding retroviral-like capsid proteins.
source: However, this form of transfer is probably limited to a small set of mRNAs encoding retroviral-like capsid proteins.
evidence: This is an inference based on the mechanism requiring specific capsid-encoding proteins.

claim: Full-length messenger RNA (mRNA) molecules can transfer between mammalian cells via tunneling nanotubes (TNTs) (Haimovich et al., 2017; Haimovich and Gerst, 2019).
source: Our lab has shown that full-length messenger RNA (mRNA) molecules can transfer between mammalian cells, but do so via tunneling nanotubes (TNTs) (Haimovich et al., 2017; Haimovich and Gerst, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to the authors' previous work.

claim: TNTs are cytoplasmic connections extending between cells that are thinner and longer than other dynamic cellular protrusions, such as lamellipodia and filopodia (Cordero Cervantes and Zurzolo, 2021).
source: TNTs are cytoplasmic connections extending between cells that are thinner and longer than other dynamic cellular protrusions, such as lamellipodia and filopodia (Cordero Cervantes and Zurzolo, 2021).

source: TNTs, which are typically 0.2–1 µm in diameter and up to >150 µm long, were shown to transfer organelles (Goodman et al., 2019; Kolba et al., 2019; Murray and Krasnodembskaya, 2019; Wang et al., 2011; Zou et al., 2020), bacteria (Kim et al., 2019; Onfelt et al., 2006), viruses (Eugenin et al., 2009; Guo et al., 2016; Panasiuk et al., 2018; Roberts et al., 2015; Tiwari et al., 2021), proteins (Biran et al., 2015), and microRNAs (Lu et al., 2019; Valadi et al., 2007).

source: TNTs have been reported to be involved in a multitude of biological processes, such as stem cell differentiation, immune response, and neurodegenerative diseases, among others (Abounit et al., 2016; Reichert et al., 2016; Zhu et al., 2021).

claim: Published RNA-sequencing data and qPCR analysis were used to detect exosome-independent transfer of keratinocyte-specific mRNAs to Langerhans cells (Su and Igyártó, 2019).
source: In addition to our work (Haimovich et al., 2017; Haimovich and Gerst, 2019), published RNA-sequencing data and qPCR analysis were used to detect exosome-independent transfer of keratinocyte-specific mRNAs to Langerhans cells (Su and Igyártó, 2019), and GFP and GNAT1 mRNAs were shown to transfer in vivo in a photoreceptor transplantation model (Ortin-Martinez et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: GFP and GNAT1 mRNAs were shown to transfer in vivo in a photoreceptor transplantation model (Ortin-Martinez et al., 2021).
source: In addition to our work (Haimovich et al., 2017; Haimovich and Gerst, 2019), published RNA-sequencing data and qPCR analysis were used to detect exosome-independent transfer of keratinocyte-specific mRNAs to Langerhans cells (Su and Igyártó, 2019), and GFP and GNAT1 mRNAs were shown to transfer in vivo in a photoreceptor transplantation model (Ortin-Martinez et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: Several full-length endogenous or ectopically expressed mRNAs undergo intercellular transfer between a variety of cell types, including immortalized cells, primary cells, and even human-mouse cell co-cultures.
source: Using this approach, we found that several full-length endogenous or ectopically expressed mRNAs undergo intercellular transfer between a variety of cell types, including immortalized cells, primary cells, and even human-mouse cell co-cultures.
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' previous work using smFISH.

claim: The level of transfer was often <1% of the endogenously expressed message in donor cells.
source: While the level of transfer was often <1% of the endogenously expressed message in donor cells, the most abundantly transferred mRNA was that of β-actin mRNA, which transferred at a level of up to 5% in some experiments.
evidence: This is based on the authors' previous findings.

claim: β-actin mRNA transferred at a level of up to 5% in some experiments.
source: While the level of transfer was often <1% of the endogenously expressed message in donor cells, the most abundantly transferred mRNA was that of β-actin mRNA, which transferred at a level of up to 5% in some experiments.
evidence: This is based on the authors' previous findings.

claim: Transfer is influenced by the identity of the donor cell, by the expression level of the RNA in donor cells and by stress conditions.
source: Initial analyses showed that transfer is influenced by the identity of the donor cell, by the expression level of the RNA in donor cells and by stress conditions.
evidence: This is based on the authors' previous findings.

claim: The transfer of mRNAs is inhibited by both cytoskeletal and small GTPase inhibitors, as well as by the binding of multiple MS2 coat proteins (MCPs) to a 24xMS2 stem-loop aptamer sequence in the mRNA (Haimovich et al., 2017).
source: We further found that the transfer of mRNAs is inhibited by both cytoskeletal and small GTPase inhibitors, as well as by the binding of multiple MS2 coat proteins (MCPs) to a 24xMS2 stem-loop aptamer sequence in the mRNA (Haimovich et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: Inhibition by the MS2 system could be explained by extensive MCP binding and hindrance to transfer or by interference with a yet-to-be-identified protein that may coat the transferred mRNA (Haimovich and Gerst, 2019).
source: Inhibition by the MS2 system could be explained by extensive MCP binding and hindrance to transfer or by interference with a yet-to-be-identified protein that may coat the transferred mRNA (Haimovich and Gerst, 2019).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation cited from the authors' previous work.

claim: Nearly all mRNAs transfer in a manner that strongly correlates with the donor cell expression level.
source: By employing deep sequencing, we found that nearly all mRNAs transfer and in a manner that strongly correlates with the donor cell expression level.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data showing correlation coefficients >0.9 (Figure 2E-G).

claim: Increasing gene expression using reporter mRNAs results in increased transfer.
source: Moreover, by increasing gene expression using reporter mRNAs we could verify that increased expression results in increased transfer.
evidence: This is supported by experiments with tdTomato reporters (Figure 5).

claim: The overall level of transfer was found to be <1% of the expression level in the donor cells.
source: Similar to our previous findings (Haimovich et al., 2017), the overall level of transfer was found to be <1% of the expression level in the donor cells and was dependent upon cell-cell contact.
evidence: This is supported by the median percentage of transfer being 0.34% (Figure 3A).

claim: Transfer was dependent upon cell-cell contact.
source: Similar to our previous findings (Haimovich et al., 2017), the overall level of transfer was found to be <1% of the expression level in the donor cells and was dependent upon cell-cell contact.
evidence: This is supported by quadrapod and conditioned media experiments (Figure 6-figure supplement 1).

claim: Neither bioinformatics search for EV-targeting motifs nor fusion of β-actin segments to a reporter revealed the presence of an element that enhances RNA transfer.
source: However, neither approach revealed the presence of an element that enhances RNA transfer, indicating that the process is inherently non-selective.
evidence: This is supported by motif analysis (Figure 5-figure supplement 2) and β-actin fragment experiments (Figure 5-figure supplement 1).

claim: The process of RNA transfer is inherently non-selective.
source: However, neither approach revealed the presence of an element that enhances RNA transfer, indicating that the process is inherently non-selective.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of specific transfer-promoting motifs and the correlation with expression level.

claim: RNA transfer is likely to be contact-dependent via TNTs, as shown for a few example mRNAs.
source: We used imaging and a Transwell-like system (i.e. quadrapod), to show that RNA transfer is likely to be contact-dependent via TNTs, as shown for a few example mRNAs.
evidence: This is supported by quadrapod experiments (Figure 6-figure supplement 1) and FISH imaging of TNTs (Figure 6).

claim: Between 90–92% of the reads were uniquely aligned to the respective reference genomes.
source: Between 90–92% of the reads were uniquely aligned to the respective reference genomes, which is an indicative of the high quality of library preparation and it was either at par or better than typical unique alignment rates (Mortazavi et al., 2008; Sarantopoulou et al., 2019; Sun et al., 2013; Zhao et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a direct measurement from the RNA-seq data analysis.

claim: More than 14,000 mouse and 16,000 human genes were annotated to their respective RefSeq database.
source: More than 14,000 mouse and 16,000 human genes were annotated to their respective RefSeq database.
evidence: This is a direct result from the RNA-seq data analysis.

claim: The percentage of unique human-aligned reads in Co-culture samples was substantially greater than in Mix samples (approximately 1.55% versus 1.13%).

evidence: This is a direct measurement from the RNA-seq data.

claim: The true proportion of unique human reads in the Mix versus the Co-culture samples was 0.075% and 0.495%, respectively, giving a read ratio that was 6.6-fold higher for MEFs in Co-culture versus MEFs in the Mix.
source: Thus, the true proportion of unique human reads in the Mix versus the Co-culture samples was 0.075% and 0.495%, respectively, giving a read ratio that was 6.6-fold higher for MEFs in Co-culture versus MEFs in the Mix.
evidence: This is calculated from the RNA-seq data after background subtraction.

claim: 10,566 transcripts of human genes were detected in Co-culture-derived or Mix-derived mouse-enriched samples.
source: In total, 10,566 transcripts of human genes were detected in Co-culture-derived or Mix-derived mouse-enriched samples (Figure 2A; Source data 1 - table 2).
evidence: This is a direct count from the RNA-seq data.

claim: 7,504 genes had RPM counts of more than 10 in both co-culture replicates.
source: Of those, 7,504 genes had RPM counts of more than 10 in both co-culture replicates (Source data 1 - table 2), of which 7501 genes had a fold-change (FC) of >1 (i.e. more reads in the Co-culture vs Mix), and 6827 genes had FC of >2 (Source data 1 - table 2).
evidence: This is a direct count from the RNA-seq data.

claim: 7501 genes had a fold-change (FC) of >1 (i.e. more reads in the Co-culture vs Mix).
source: Of those, 7,504 genes had RPM counts of more than 10 in both co-culture replicates (Source data 1 - table 2), of which 7501 genes had a fold-change (FC) of >1 (i.e. more reads in the Co-culture vs Mix), and 6827 genes had FC of >2 (Source data 1 - table 2).
evidence: This is a direct count from the RNA-seq data.

claim: 6827 genes had FC of >2.

evidence: This is a direct count from the RNA-seq data.

claim: Human β-actin mRNA was significantly enriched in the MBS-MEFs after co-culture, as confirmed by RT-PCR and qRT-PCR.
source: Both detection methods revealed a significant enrichment of human β-actin mRNA in the MBS-MEFs after co-culture.
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR and qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1C and D.

claim: 283 mRNAs robustly transferred from human (MCF7) cells to mouse (MBS-MEF) cells with a fold-change of more than 2.
source: By employing a single-tailed unpaired t-test, we found that 283 mRNAs robustly transferred from human (MCF7) cells to mouse (MBS-MEF) cells with a fold-change of more than 2 (Figure 2D, Source data 1 - table 3).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Many of the identified transferred mRNAs included cytoskeletal components (ACTB, ACTG), translation factors (EEF1A1, EEF2), ribosomal proteins (RPL8, RPL4, RPL7) and other 'housekeeping' genes (GAPDH, PABPC1).
source: Many of the identified mRNAs included cytoskeletal components (ACTB, ACTG), translation factors (EEF1A1, EEF2), ribosomal proteins (RPL8, RPL4, RPL7) and other 'housekeeping' genes (GAPDH, PABPC1).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the 283 robustly transferred genes.

claim: mRNAs encoding multiple types of keratins (e.g. KRT8, 18, 19, and 80) were identified among transferred mRNAs, similar to those reported to transfer from keratinocytes to epidermal-resident Langerhans cells (Su and Igyártó, 2019).
source: Among this group we also identified mRNAs encoding multiple types of keratins (e.g. KRT8, 18, 19, and 80), similar to those reported to transfer from keratinocytes to epidermal-resident Langerhans cells (Su and Igyártó, 2019).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the 283 robustly transferred genes and comparison to published literature.

claim: The number of transferred human RNAs strongly correlated with their expression levels (Pearson and Spearman coefficients >0.9).
source: We found that the number of transferred human RNAs strongly correlated with their expression levels (Pearson and Spearman coefficients >0.9; Figure 2F), most falling within the 99% confidence interval of the regression.
evidence: This is based on linear regression analysis shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The level of gene expression prior to co-culture can be a dominant predictor of RNA transfer.
source: This indicates that the level of gene expression prior to co-culture can be a dominant predictor of RNA transfer.
evidence: This is an inference based on the strong correlation between expression and transfer.

claim: A strong correlation was observed between ACTB-MBS expression levels and ACTB-MBS mRNA transfer when comparing between immortalized and primary donor MBS-MEFs (Haimovich et al., 2017).
source: Likewise, a strong correlation was observed between ACTB-MBS expression levels and ACTB-MBS mRNA transfer when comparing between immortalized and primary donor MBS-MEFs (Haimovich et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: There is no correlation between endogenous RNA expression in donor cells to the log2FC of human RNAs in co-cultured cells when looking at the whole transcriptome (Pearson coefficient = 0.07).
source: When looking at the whole transcriptome, we found no correlation between endogenous RNA expression in donor cells to the log2FC of human RNAs in co-cultured cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Pearson coefficient = 0.07).
evidence: This is based on correlation analysis shown in Figure 2-figure supplement 1.

claim: Mitochondria-encoded RNAs (e.g. 13 mRNAs and 2 rRNAs) showed poor transfer (log2FC = 0.03–0.45) despite their high expression.
source: We noted that unlike the 283 robustly expressed and transferred RNAs described above, mitochondria-encoded RNAs (e.g. 13 mRNAs and 2 rRNAs) showed poor transfer (log2FC = 0.03–0.45) despite their high expression.
evidence: This is based on analysis of RNA-seq data for mitochondrial genes.

claim: The median percentage of transfer for all human RNAs was low [0.34%, log10 (percentage of transfer)=–0.44].
source: We further observed that the median percentage of transfer for all human RNAs was low [0.34%, log10 (percentage of transfer)=–0.44] (Figure 3A, Source data 1 - table 4).
evidence: This is based on analysis of RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The percentage of RNA transfer did not correlate linearly with gene expression.
source: Although the absolute number of transferred RNAs (using RPM as a measure) depended on gene expression level in the donor cells, the percentage of RNA transfer did not correlate linearly with gene expression (Figure 3B, Source data 1 - table 4).
evidence: This is based on linear regression analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Only a low proportion of RNAs from the mammalian transcriptome is likely to undergo transfer to neighboring cells.
source: This result indicates that only a low proportion of RNAs from the mammalian transcriptome is likely to undergo transfer to neighboring cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the low median percentage of transfer.

claim: The percentage of transfer of the total RNA population, as well as that of the group of 283 robustly transferred mRNAs, was largely independent of mRNA stability.
source: We found that the percentage of transfer of the total RNA population, as well as that of the group of 283 robustly transferred mRNAs, was largely independent of mRNA stability (Figure 3C, Source data 1 - table 5).
evidence: This is based on correlation analysis with published mRNA half-life data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The transfer of mRNAs from 12 primate-specific genes (e.g. DHRS4L2, GTF2H2C, NBPF10, NBPF14, ALG1L, CBWD2, APOL2, ZNF43, ZNF726, ZNF816, ZNF680, and ZNF718) was detected in co-cultured MEFs.
source: Interestingly, we could also detect the transfer of mRNAs from 12 primate-specific genes (e.g. DHRS4L2, GTF2H2C, NBPF10, NBPF14, ALG1L, CBWD2, APOL2, ZNF43, ZNF726, ZNF816, ZNF680, and ZNF718) in co-cultured MEFs.

source: These genes are highly expressed in cortical regions of primate brains and are not reported to have any mouse orthologues (Florio et al., 2018).

claim: 174 lncRNAs were detected in MCF7 Single cultures (out of 5301 known lncRNAs).
source: We detected the expression of 174 lncRNAs in MCF7 Single cultures (out of 5301 known lncRNAs) and identified 102 having >10 RPM in Coculture samples - 100 of which were transferred with a FC >2 (Source data 1 - table 7).

claim: 102 lncRNAs had >10 RPM in Coculture samples - 100 of which were transferred with a FC >2.
source: We detected the expression of 174 lncRNAs in MCF7 Single cultures (out of 5301 known lncRNAs) and identified 102 having >10 RPM in Coculture samples - 100 of which were transferred with a FC >2 (Source data 1 - table 7).

claim: 5 lncRNAs were among the most highly endogenously expressed genes in MCF7 cells and amongst the 283 robustly transferred RNAs.
source: We noted that 5 lncRNAs were among the most highly endogenously expressed genes in MCF7 cells and amongst the 283 robustly transferred RNAs (Source data 1 - table 3).

claim: mRNAs corresponding to 40 breast cancer-related overexpressed genes and 77 breast cancer-related mutated genes underwent transfer from MCF7 to MBS-MEF cells.
source: We found that mRNAs corresponding to 40 breast cancer-related overexpressed genes and 77 breast cancer-related mutated genes underwent transfer from MCF7 to MBS-MEF cells (=0.074 and p<3.776e-13, respectively, using a hypergeometric test) (Figure 3D; Source data 1 - table 8).

claim: One gene (BUB1B) was found to be both overexpressed and mutated, and to undergo transfer.
source: One gene (BUB1B) was found to be both overexpressed and mutated, and to undergo transfer.
evidence: This is based on analysis of RNA-seq data and comparison with breast cancer gene lists.

claim: The robust transfer of RNAs shown by sequencing could be verified using qRT-PCR for 10 highly transferred genes.
source: In full agreement with the RNA-seq results (Figure 2), the robust transfer of RNAs shown by sequencing could also be verified using qRT-PCR (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is based on qRT-PCR validation shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The transfer of KRT8, PSAP and CCND1 mRNAs from MCF7 cells to MBS-MEF cells was validated using smFISH.
source: In parallel, we validated the transfer of a set of highly transferred mRNAs using smFISH for three genes (e.g. KRT8, PSAP and CCND1) in MBS-MEF cells using human-specific FISH probes (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: This is based on smFISH experiments shown in Figure 4B and C.

claim: The transfer of KRT8 mRNA was noticeably higher than that of CCND1 or PSAP, which might be attributed to the higher expression of KRT8 in MCF7 cells.
source: As expected, the transfer of KRT8 mRNA was noticeably higher than that of CCND1 or PSAP, which might be attributed to the higher expression of KRT8 in MCF7 cells.
evidence: This is based on smFISH quantification and is consistent with expression-dependent transfer.

claim: Most of the transferred mRNAs were involved in translation initiation, RNA transport, ribosome biogenesis and mRNA splicing.
source: We found that most of the mRNAs were involved in translation initiation, RNA transport, ribosome biogenesis and mRNA splicing (Figure 2—figure supplement 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is based on GO term analysis of the 283 robustly transferred genes.

claim: In terms of molecular functions, transferred mRNAs encoded for poly-A binding proteins, ribosomal proteins and translation factors and localizing to the cytosol, cell membrane or ribosome.
source: In terms of molecular functions, transferred mRNAs encoded for poly-A binding proteins, ribosomal proteins and translation factors and localizing to the cytosol, cell membrane or ribosome (Figure 2—figure supplement 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is based on GO term analysis of the 283 robustly transferred genes.

claim: The transferred mRNAs were enriched for pathways such as RNA transport, metabolism, translation and rRNA processing.
source: The transferred mRNAs were enriched for pathways such as RNA transport, metabolism, translation and rRNA processing (Figure 2—figure supplement 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is based on KEGG and Reactome pathway analysis of the 283 robustly transferred genes.

claim: tdTomato-low expression cells expressed an average 429 molecules of tdTomato mRNAs, out of which, an average of 7 molecules (~1.6%) were transferred to WT-MEF acceptor cells.
source: tdTomato-low expression cells were found to express an average 429 molecules of tdTomato mRNAs, out of which, an average of 7 molecules (~1.6%) were transferred to WT-MEF acceptor cells (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is based on smFISH quantification shown in Figure 5B.

claim: tdTomato-high expression cells expressed an average of 1250 molecules of tdTomato mRNA, of which 25 molecules (2%) were able to transfer.
source: On the other hand, tdTomato-high expression cells were found to express an average of 1250 molecules of tdTomato mRNA, of which 25 molecules (2%) were able to transfer (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is based on smFISH quantification shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Higher concentrations of Doxycycline (4 µg/ml) induced a higher level of tdTomato mRNA expression (average = 492 copies/cell) and, consequently, transferred more mRNA to the acceptor cells (average: 1.5 copies/cell) than lower levels of Doxycycline (2 µg/ml; average expression = 165 copies per cell;<1 transferred).
source: Higher concentrations of Doxycycline (4 µg/ml) induced a higher level of tdTomato mRNA expression (average = 492 copies/cell) and, consequently, transferred more mRNA to the acceptor cells (average: 1.5 copies/cell) than lower levels of Doxycycline (2 µg/ml; average expression = 165 copies per cell;<1 transferred; Figure 5C).
evidence: This is based on smFISH quantification of doxycycline-inducible tdTomato shown in Figure 5C.

claim: tdTomato mRNA alone transferred at a higher level than that of the fusion constructs with β-actin fragments.
source: Next, we examined RNA transfer (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D, Supplementary file 1 - table 2) and found that tdTomato mRNA alone transferred at a higher level than that of the fusion constructs, although the fusions amongst themselves showed similar levels of transfer.
evidence: This is based on smFISH quantification shown in Figure 5-figure supplement 1D.

claim: No fragment of β-actin that promotes mRNA transfer was identified in the context of fusion to tdTomato 3'UTR and ectopic expression.
source: Thus, we could not identify a fragment of β-actin that promotes mRNA transfer, at least in the context of this assay, that is placed in the 3'UTR of tdTomato and expressed ectopically.
evidence: This is based on the experimental results showing no enhanced transfer with β-actin fragments.

claim: Three different purine-rich motifs were enriched in the coding sequences of nearly all highly transferred mRNAs.
source: While no such motif was detected at the level of amino acid sequences or in the UTRs, three different purine-rich motifs were enriched in the coding sequences of nearly all mRNAs (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is based on MEME Suite analysis shown in Figure 5-figure supplement 2A.

claim: Two motifs contain the sequence 5'–GAAGAAG-3', which is similar to the 5'–GCAGAAG-3' or 5'–GGAGAAG-3' sequences present in each of the coding sequence fragments of β-actin.
source: Two contain the sequence 5'–GAAGAAG-3', which is similar to the 5'–GCAGAAG-3' or 5'–GGAGAAG-3' sequences present in each of the coding sequence fragments of β-actin, described above, but did not show enhanced transfer (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is based on motif analysis and comparison with β-actin fragment experiments.

claim: All three sets of poorly transferred genes contained similar purine-rich sequences as found in the highly transferred genes with the 5'–GAAGAAG-3' motif identifiable in Sets 2 and 3.
source: Interestingly, all three sets contained similar purine-rich sequences as found in the highly transferred genes with the 5'–GAAGAAG-3' motif identifiable in Sets 2 and 3 (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is based on MEME Suite analysis of poorly transferred genes shown in Figure 5-figure supplement 2B.

claim: The 5'–GAAGAAG-3' sequence is unlikely to be a transfer-promoting feature as it is not specific to highly transferred genes.
source: As this sequence is not specific to highly transferred genes it is unlikely to be a transfer-promoting feature.
evidence: This is an inference based on the presence of the motif in both highly and poorly transferred genes.

claim: One EV-targeting motif is completely absent from the robustly transferred mRNA cohort, as well as from control cohorts.
source: However, we found that one motif is completely absent from this cohort, as well as from our three control cohorts described above.
evidence: This is based on FIMO analysis of EV-targeting motifs.

claim: Four EV-targeting motifs were found in only 10–19% of the robustly transferred mRNAs, but were present at a similar level (10–25%) in control sets.
source: The other four motifs were found in only 10–19% of the robustly transferred mRNAs, but were present at a similar level (10–25%) in our control sets (Supplementary file 1 - table 3).
evidence: This is based on FIMO analysis of EV-targeting motifs.

claim: None of the three approaches could conclusively identify cis elements that might promote RNA selection for transfer.
source: Thus, none of the three approaches could conclusively identify cis elements that might promote RNA selection for transfer.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the negative results from β-actin fragment experiments, motif analysis, and EV-motif analysis.

claim: The transfer of both β-actin and GFP mRNAs was completely abrogated when donor and acceptor cells were separated in space (e.g. using a tripod/transwell setup) or when the acceptor cells were treated with donor cell-derived conditioned medium (Haimovich et al., 2017).
source: The transfer of both β-actin and GFP mRNAs was completely abrogated when donor and acceptor cells were separated in space (e.g. using a tripod/transwell setup) or when the acceptor cells were treated with donor cell-derived conditioned medium (Haimovich et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: The transfer of mRNAs was found to be highest in the Co-culture samples as compared to the quadrapod or conditioned media-treated samples across two independent replicates.
source: The transfer of mRNAs was found to be highest in the Co-culture samples as compared to the quadrapod or conditioned media-treated samples across two independent replicates (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is based on qRT-PCR analysis shown in Figure 6-figure supplement 1B.

claim: The mRNAs did not transfer by diffusion (e.g. either by secreted vesicles or ribonucleoprotein complexes), but requires cell-cell contact.
source: This indicates that the mRNAs did not transfer by diffusion (e.g. either by secreted vesicles or ribonucleoprotein complexes), but requires cell-cell contact.
evidence: This is an inference based on the quadrapod and conditioned media experiments.

claim: Contact-dependent transfer is likely to be the predominant mechanism for transcriptome-wide mRNA transfer.
source: As the genes selected for this experiment encode diverse biological functions and do not belong to any common pathway, it suggests that contact-dependent transfer is likely to be the predominant mechanism for transcriptome-wide mRNA transfer.
evidence: This is an inference based on the diversity of genes tested in the quadrapod experiment.

claim: Both MEF and MCF7 cell types produce TNTs which connect between MEFs-MEFs, MCF7-MCF7 and MEFs-MCF7 cells.
source: We found that both cell types produce TNTs which connect between MEFs-MEFs, MCF7-MCF7 and MEFs-MCF7 cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on live imaging of membrane-labeled cells shown in Figure 6-figure supplement 2.

claim: MCF7 cells were found connected by TNTs to other MCF7 cells or to MEFs, and most of these TNTs contained FISH spots representing KRT8 mRNA or CCND1 mRNA.
source: Nevertheless, we found a few examples of MCF7 cells connected by TNTs to other MCF7 cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 3A, B), or to MEFs (Figure 6—figure supplement 3C–E). Most of these TNTs contained FISH spots that represent KRT8 mRNA (Figure 6—figure supplement 3A–C) or CCND1 mRNA (Figure 6—figure supplement 3E).
evidence: This is based on smFISH imaging shown in Figure 6-figure supplement 3.

claim: KRT8 and CCND1 mRNAs were observed in actin-containing long protrusions that run above the substratum and connect two cells – key features of TNTs.
source: Figure 6 and Figure 6—video 1 and Figure 6—video 2 show two examples of KRT8 or CCND1 mRNAs in actin-containing long protrusions that run above the substratum and connect two cells – key features of TNTs (Ljubojevic et al., 2021).
evidence: This is based on smFISH with phalloidin staining shown in Figure 6.

claim: mRNA transfer in the co-culture system likely occurs via TNTs.
source: Together with the results presented in Figure 6—figure supplement 1, we conclude that mRNA transfer in our co-culture system likely occurs via TNTs.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on multiple lines of evidence including contact-dependence and visualization of mRNAs in TNTs.

claim: The mouse transcriptome in Co-culture samples was significantly different from that of the Mix and Single cultures.
source: RNA-seq analysis revealed that the mouse transcriptome in Co-culture samples was significantly different from that of the Mix and Single cultures, which cluster together and have very similar transcriptomic profiles (Figure 7A and B).
evidence: This is based on heatmap and PCA analysis shown in Figure 7A and B.

claim: MBS-MEFs undergo stark changes in gene expression upon co-culture with MCF7 cells.
source: This indicates that MBS-MEFs undergo stark changes in gene expression upon co-culture with MCF7 cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential transcriptome analysis.

claim: More than 4000 genes are ≥2 fold differentially expressed in MEFs upon co-culture, including ~1000 upregulated genes and ~3000 downregulated genes.
source: We detected more than 4000 genes that are ≥2 fold differentially expressed, including ~1000 upregulated genes and ~3000 downregulated genes (Figure 7C) (Source data 1 - table 9).
evidence: This is based on differential gene expression analysis shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Tenascin-C (TNC), a cancer-associated fibroblast (CAF) marker, was upregulated ~3.5-fold in the MEF-enriched fraction of the Co-culture sample.
source: Interestingly, we observed the ~3.5-fold upregulation of a cancer-associated fibroblast (CAF) marker, Tenascin-C (TNC) (Ni et al., 2017), in the MEF-enriched fraction of the Co-culture sample (Source data 1 - table 9).
evidence: This is based on differential gene expression analysis.

claim: MEFs might become CAF-like when co-cultured with a cancer cell line (e.g. MCF7 cells).
source: This raises the speculation that MEFs might become CAF-like when co-cultured with a cancer cell line (e.g. MCF7 cells).
evidence: This is speculation based on the upregulation of CAF markers.

claim: 30 upregulated and 17 downregulated genes were conserved between MEFs in co-culture and CAFs (versus their precursor mesenchymal stem cells - MSCs).
source: Interestingly, we found 30 upregulated and 17 downregulated genes conserved between the two datasets (Figure 8A, Source data 1 - table 10).
evidence: This is based on comparison with published CAF gene expression data shown in Figure 8.

claim: Among upregulated genes in the MEFs, multiple extracellular-matrix associated genes (e.g. ACTA1, ACTA2, COL6A3, ADAM12, ADAM19) were also upregulated in CAFs associated with metastatic lung cancer.
source: Among upregulated genes in the MEFs, multiple extracellular-matrix associated genes (e.g. ACTA1, ACTA2, COL6A3, ADAM12, ADAM19) were also upregulated in CAFs associated with metastatic lung cancer (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is based on comparison with published CAF gene expression data shown in Figure 8.

claim: Mouse KRT8, which is frequently associated with apical CAFs (apCAFs) in the breast and pancreatic cancer microenvironment (Elyada et al., 2019; Sebastian et al., 2020), was upregulated in MEFs in response to co-culture with MCF7 cells.
source: Furthermore, mouse KRT8, which is frequently associated with apical CAFs (apCAFs) in the breast and pancreatic cancer microenvironment (Elyada et al., 2019; Sebastian et al., 2020) was upregulated in MEFs in response to co-culture with MCF7 cells (Source data 1 - table 9).
evidence: This is based on differential gene expression analysis and comparison with published literature.

claim: Co-culture with human cancer cells might lead to CAF-like phenotypes in cultured fibroblasts.
source: This indicates that co-culture with human cancer cells might lead to CAF-like phenotypes in cultured fibroblasts.
evidence: This is an inference based on the upregulation of multiple CAF markers and pathways.

claim: Top upregulated pathways in MEFs upon co-culture included 'Ribosome biogenesis in eukaryotes', 'RNA transport' and 'Focal adhesion'.
source: Top upregulated pathways included 'Ribosome biogenesis in eukaryotes', 'RNA transport' and 'Focal adhesion', while top downregulated pathways included signaling pathways, such as 'Calcium Signaling pathway' and 'Rap1 signaling pathway' (Figure 7—figure supplement 1, Figure 7—figure supplement 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is based on KEGG pathway analysis shown in Figure 7-figure supplement 1.

claim: Top downregulated pathways in MEFs upon co-culture included 'Calcium Signaling pathway' and 'Rap1 signaling pathway'.
source: Top upregulated pathways included 'Ribosome biogenesis in eukaryotes', 'RNA transport' and 'Focal adhesion', while top downregulated pathways included signaling pathways, such as 'Calcium Signaling pathway' and 'Rap1 signaling pathway' (Figure 7—figure supplement 1, Figure 7—figure supplement 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is based on KEGG pathway analysis shown in Figure 7-figure supplement 1.

claim: Many cancer-related pathways (e.g. MAPK signaling, Ras signaling) were found to be upregulated in MEFs upon co-culture.
source: Upon close observation, many cancer-related pathways (e.g. MAPK signaling, Ras signaling) were found to be upregulated, while pathways such as cytokine-cytokine interactions and transcriptional misregulation in cancer were downregulated (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is based on pathway analysis shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Pathways such as cytokine-cytokine interactions and transcriptional misregulation in cancer were downregulated in MEFs upon co-culture.
source: Upon close observation, many cancer-related pathways (e.g. MAPK signaling, Ras signaling) were found to be upregulated, while pathways such as cytokine-cytokine interactions and transcriptional misregulation in cancer were downregulated (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is based on pathway analysis shown in Figure 7C.

claim: 'ECM-Receptor interaction' pathway was found to be both up- and downregulated in MBS-MEFs in response to co-culture with MCF7 cells.
source: Another major cancer-related pathway, 'ECM-Receptor interaction' was found to be both up- and downregulated in MBS-MEFs in response to co-culture with MCF7 cells (Figure 7C), with most of the upregulated genes associated with poly-A RNA binding, translation initiation, ribosome biogenesis and ribosome assembly-related GO terms (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on pathway analysis shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Cell immunity-related genes were significantly downregulated in MEFs upon co-culture.
source: Interestingly, cell immunity-related genes were significantly downregulated, leading to speculation that RNA transfer and/or co-culture modulates the immune response of acceptor cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is based on GO term analysis shown in Figure 7-figure supplement 1D.

claim: RNA transfer and/or co-culture may modulate the immune response of acceptor cells.
source: Interestingly, cell immunity-related genes were significantly downregulated, leading to speculation that RNA transfer and/or co-culture modulates the immune response of acceptor cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is speculation based on the downregulation of immunity-related genes.

claim: The level of gene expression alone explains more than 90% of RNA transfer.
source: We found that the level of gene expression alone explains more than 90% of RNA transfer (Figure 2E–G and Figure 5).
evidence: This is based on the high correlation coefficients (>0.9) observed in linear regression analyses.

claim: Transfer of human Cyclin D1 mRNA and mouse β-actin mRNA correlates with the expression level in donor cells (Haimovich et al., 2017).
source: This is in agreement with our previous finding that transfer of human Cyclin D1 mRNA and mouse β-actin mRNA correlates with the expression level in donor cells (Haimovich et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: The amount of transferred RNAs (as quantified by PCR) positively correlated with gene expression in a study reporting transfer of keratinocyte-associated mRNAs to Langerhans cells (Su and Igyártó, 2019).
source: Another study, that reported transfer of keratinocyte-associated mRNAs to Langerhans cells, mostly through a contact-dependent mechanism, also found that the amount of transferred RNAs (as quantified by PCR) positively correlated with gene expression (Su and Igyártó, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: Long-distance transport of mRNAs in Arabidopsis was largely non-selective and dependent on gene expression (Calderwood et al., 2016; Hofmann, 2016).
source: An analysis of mRNAs exhibiting long-distance transport in Arabidopsis showed that was largely non-selective and dependent on gene expression (Calderwood et al., 2016; Hofmann, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies in plants.

claim: In host-parasitic plant RNA transfer, a large proportion of host and parasite mRNAs were found in each other's tissues in an expression-dependent manner (Notaguchi et al., 2015).
source: In case of RNA transfer between species, such as host-parasitic plants, a large proportion of host and parasite mRNAs were found in each other's tissues in an expression-dependent manner (Notaguchi et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: In cross-species grafting, no specific cis motif was found among Arabidopsis mRNAs that were found in Nicotiana tissues (Notaguchi et al., 2015).
source: In an instance of cross-species grafting, no specific cis motif was found among Arabidopsis mRNAs that were found in Nicotiana tissues (Notaguchi et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: RNA modification [5-methyl cytosine (m5C)] mainly in the proximal end of coding regions was responsible for transport of certain mRNAs from shoot to root of Arabidopsis (Yang et al., 2019).
source: However, a recent report found that RNA modification [5-methyl cytosine (m5C)] mainly in the proximal end of coding regions was responsible for transport of certain mRNAs from shoot to root of Arabidopsis (Yang et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: A tRNA-like structure or actual bi-cistronic mRNA-tRNA transcript acts as a cis-acting element in plant mRNA transfer (Huang and Yu, 2009; Zhang et al., 2016).
source: In addition, two works describe a tRNA-like structure or actual bi-cistronic mRNA-tRNA transcript that acts as a cis-acting element in plant mRNA transfer (Huang and Yu, 2009; Zhang et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: HER2 mRNA transfer from two human cell lines (e.g. NCI-N87 and SKBR3 cells) to MEFs was similar, although the expression level in SKBR3 cells was 2-fold higher (Haimovich et al., 2017).
source: On the other hand, we showed previously that the level of contact-dependent mRNA transfer can depend on cell type, as HER2 mRNA transfer from two human cell lines (e.g. NCI-N87 and SKBR3 cells) to MEFs was similar, although the expression level in SKBR3 cells was 2-fold higher (Haimovich et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: RNA transfer might correlate with endogenous expression levels within the same cell type, but not necessarily across different cell types.
source: Thus, RNA transfer might correlate with endogenous expression levels within the same cell type, but not necessarily across different cell types.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that transfer efficiency can vary between cell types despite similar expression levels.

claim: The existence of transfer-inhibiting or -promoting elements recognized by cell-type specific factors could provide a possible explanation why some cell types transfer certain mRNAs or lncRNAs better or worse than others.
source: The existence of transfer-inhibiting or -promoting elements recognized by cell-type specific factors could provide a possible explanation why some cell types transfer certain mRNAs or lncRNAs better or worse than others, even when taking gene expression levels and growth conditions (e.g. stress conditions or presence of extracellular matrix proteins, like fibronectin) into consideration.
evidence: This is speculation about potential mechanisms.

claim: A report characterizing the transcriptome of the EV populations derived from hepatic cancer cell lines identified 238 protein-coding mRNAs and 35 lncRNAs, in addition to numerous miRNAs and snoRNAs (Berardocco et al., 2017).
source: Interestingly, a report characterizing the transcriptome of the EV populations derived from hepatic cancer cell lines identified 238 protein-coding mRNAs and 35 lncRNAs, in addition to numerous miRNAs and snoRNAs (Berardocco et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: Many mRNAs found in hepatic EVs were found to be highly transferred in this study and included genes encoding ribosomal proteins, ACTG, ACTB, and EEF2.
source: Many of these mRNAs were found to be highly transferred here and included genes encoding ribosomal proteins, ACTG, ACTB, and EEF2, etc.
evidence: This is based on comparison of the current study's results with published EV transcriptome data.

claim: mRNAs or mRNA fragments might be transferred by hepatic EVs and the loading of RNAs into such vesicles may be expression-dependent (He et al., 2015; Berardocco et al., 2017).
source: Along with an earlier work (He et al., 2015), it implies that mRNAs or mRNA fragments might be transferred by hepatic EVs and that the loading of RNAs into such vesicles may be expression-dependent.
evidence: This is speculation based on comparison with published EV studies.

claim: The average percentage of transfer of ACTB, KRT8, PSAP and CCND1 mRNA as assayed using FISH is 5–10 fold higher than the estimate from RNA-seq.
source: For example, the average percentage of transfer of ACTB, KRT8, PSAP and CCND1 mRNA as assayed using FISH is 5–10 fold higher than the estimate from RNA-seq (i.e. compare data in Figure 4C to that in Source data 1 - table 4).
evidence: This is based on comparison of FISH and RNA-seq quantification.

claim: Trypsinization and re-plating of acceptor MEFs leads to a massive loss in transferred ACTB-MBS mRNA, possibly through degradation.
source: We have observed that the trypsinization and re-plating of acceptor MEFs leads to a massive loss in transferred ACTB-MBS mRNA, possibly through degradation (data not shown).
evidence: This is based on unpublished observations by the authors.

claim: RNA-seq library preparation may introduce bias in the detection of high abundance transcripts versus lower abundance ones at the reverse transcription and/or amplification levels.
source: On the other hand, RNA-seq library preparation may introduce bias in the detection of high abundance transcripts versus lower abundance ones at the reverse transcription and/or amplification levels.
evidence: This is a statement of known technical limitations of RNA-seq.

claim: There is an experimental bias towards the detection of endogenous mRNAs, as compared to transferred mRNAs.
source: Thus, there is an experimental bias towards the detection of endogenous mRNAs, as compared to transferred mRNAs, and multiplex FISH methods may eventually prove more accurate.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of FISH and RNA-seq results and technical considerations.

claim: The transfer of β-actin-MBS mRNA reached a maximum within 2.5 hr, and was maintained at the same level for at least 24 hr when either immortalized or primary MBS-MEFs were co-cultured with immortalized or primary wild-type MEFs (Haimovich et al., 2017).
source: Although the transfer of β-actin-MBS mRNA reached a maximum within 2.5 hr, and was maintained at the same level for at least 24 hr when either immortalized or primary MBS-MEFs were co-cultured with immortalized or primary wild-type MEFs (Haimovich et al., 2017), the transfer of β-actin-MBS mRNA continued to increase at least for up to 12 hr when MBS-MEFs were co-cultured with MCF7 cells (Dasgupta and Gerst, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to the authors' previous work.

claim: The transfer of β-actin-MBS mRNA continued to increase at least for up to 12 hr when MBS-MEFs were co-cultured with MCF7 cells (Dasgupta and Gerst, 2020).
source: Although the transfer of β-actin-MBS mRNA reached a maximum within 2.5 hr, and was maintained at the same level for at least 24 hr when either immortalized or primary MBS-MEFs were co-cultured with immortalized or primary wild-type MEFs (Haimovich et al., 2017), the transfer of β-actin-MBS mRNA continued to increase at least for up to 12 hr when MBS-MEFs were co-cultured with MCF7 cells (Dasgupta and Gerst, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: Greater levels of accumulation of transferred RNAs might occur depending upon cell type and growth conditions, as well as the RNA transfer rate and stability in the acceptor cells.
source: Thus, greater levels of accumulation of transferred RNAs might occur depending upon cell type and growth conditions, as well as the RNA transfer rate and stability in the acceptor cells.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed variability in transfer kinetics.

claim: Mitochondria were shown to transfer through TNTs (Rustom et al., 2004; Sartori-Rupp et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2011; Zou et al., 2020).
source: Although mitochondria were shown to transfer through TNTs (Rustom et al., 2004; Sartori-Rupp et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2011; Zou et al., 2020), our RNA-seq results showed poor transfer of mitochondria-encoded RNAs relative to their expression (Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Source data 1 - table 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: TNT-mediated mitochondrial transfer may be limited using the experimental conditions of this study or may not be an efficient vehicle for RNA transfer.
source: It may be that TNT-mediated mitochondrial transfer is limited using our experimental conditions or that it may not be an efficient vehicle for transfer.
evidence: This is speculation based on the poor transfer of mitochondrial RNAs despite evidence of mitochondrial transfer via TNTs.

claim: Limited live imaging data suggests that transfer is motorized (Haimovich et al., 2017).
source: On the other hand, limited live imaging data suggests that transfer is motorized (Haimovich et al., 2017) and, thus, the RNA might require specialized packaging or modification for transfer and recognition by TNT-specific motor proteins.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: The RNA might require specialized packaging or modification for transfer and recognition by TNT-specific motor proteins.
source: On the other hand, limited live imaging data suggests that transfer is motorized (Haimovich et al., 2017) and, thus, the RNA might require specialized packaging or modification for transfer and recognition by TNT-specific motor proteins.
evidence: This is speculation based on the evidence of motorized transfer.

claim: Specialized packaging or modification may distinguish RNAs targeted for transfer from non-transferred RNAs (Haimovich and Gerst, 2019).
source: This packaging or modification may distinguish RNAs targeted for transfer from non-transferred RNAs (Haimovich and Gerst, 2019).
evidence: This is speculation cited from the authors' previous work.

claim: RNA molecules may be co-transcriptionally 'marked' for transfer, especially since mRNA fate may be determined during transcription (Dahan and Choder, 2013; Haimovich et al., 2013; Nair et al., 2021; Slobodin and Dikstein, 2020; Trcek and Singer, 2010).
source: Thus, it is tempting to speculate that RNA molecules may be co-transcriptionally 'marked' for transfer, especially since mRNA fate may be determined during transcription (Dahan and Choder, 2013; Haimovich et al., 2013; Nair et al., 2021; Slobodin and Dikstein, 2020; Trcek and Singer, 2010).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citations to studies on co-transcriptional mRNA fate determination.

claim: Transfer could be isoform-specific.
source: Alternatively, transfer could be isoform-specific.
evidence: This is speculation about a potential mechanism.

claim: The low read counts of transferred RNAs in the RNA-seq experiment may have prevented determination of whether they are enriched for specific transcription start sites, alternative poly-adenylation sites, or alternatively spliced isoforms.
source: However, the low read counts of transferred RNAs in our RNA-seq experiment may have prevented us from determining if they are enriched for specific transcription start sites, alternative poly-adenylation sites, or alternatively spliced isoforms.
evidence: This is a statement about a technical limitation of the study.

claim: Understanding the mechanism of mRNA transfer will be key to further explore its physiological importance.
source: Understanding the mechanism of mRNA transfer will be key to further explore its physiological importance.
evidence: This is a statement about future research directions.

claim: It is unlikely that some or many mRNAs transfer by means other than TNTs.
source: Although it is possible that some or many mRNAs transfer by means other than TNTs, we think it unlikely, since the results on TNT-mediated cell-to-cell transfer in both this and our previous publication (Haimovich, 2017), as well as by others (Ortin-Martinez et al., 2021; Su and Igyártó, 2019), tested a variety of mRNAs from different families and which localize to various sub-cellular localizations.
evidence: This is an inference based on the diversity of mRNAs shown to transfer via TNTs.

claim: The pathway of TNT-mediated mRNA transfer is more general than the few examples presented in this study.
source: This indicates that the pathway we have uncovered is more general than the few examples presented here.
evidence: This is an inference based on the diversity of mRNAs tested.

claim: A bioRxiv pre-print (Yingying et al., 2023) recapitulated the key findings of this study in a different human-mouse co-culture system.
source: Of note, our key findings were recently recapitulated in a different human-mouse co-culture system. In this bioRxiv pre-print (Yingying et al., 2023), the authors co-cultured human pluripotent stem cells with mouse epiblast stem cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a preprint.

claim: In the bioRxiv pre-print, the authors found a contact-dependent human-to-mouse mRNA transfer, at levels ranging from 0.33% to 1.3% for bulk RNA-seq and 1.2% for scRNA-seq.
source: In both cases, the authors found a contact-dependent human-to-mouse mRNA transfer, at levels ranging from 0.33% to 1.3% for bulk RNA-seq and 1.2% for scRNA-seq, similar to our findings presented here.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a preprint.

claim: In the bioRxiv pre-print, mRNA transfer was found to be non-specific and the rate of transfer correlated to the level of gene expression in the human donor cells.
source: Likewise, mRNA transfer was found to be non-specific and the rate of transfer correlated to the level of gene expression in the human donor cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a preprint.

claim: TNT-mediated RNA transfer may play a role in key biological processes, such as tumor growth, tissue differentiation and development.
source: The findings of this study will enable us to answer if TNT-mediated RNA transfer plays a role in key biological processes, such as tumor growth, tissue differentiation and development as investigated for EVs (Liu et al., 2018; Prieto-Vila et al., 2021; Raulf et al., 2018).
